set1.q: A 45-year-old woman taking warfarin for a mechanical valve presents with 2 days of sharp chest pain eased by leaning forward, widespread ST elevation and a small effusion. She is afebrile and her blood pressure is 128/78. Which is the most appropriate disposition?
opts: Uncomplicated low-risk pericarditis can be managed as an outpatient, but oral anticoagulation is a high-risk feature that favors admission.
ruled out by a stated finding
Discharge after one dose of ibuprofen
A single dose and discharge ignores her high-risk status on anticoagulation, which raises the danger of bleeding into the pericardium.
Delaying evaluation is unsafe for a high-risk patient; anticoagulant use favors hospital admission now.

Correct. Patients on oral anticoagulants are among the higher-risk groups for acute pericarditis (with fever, subacute course, tamponade signs, large effusion, immunosuppression, trauma, raised troponin) and potentially need hospitalization.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 64-year-old man has heart-failure-like edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. The differential is narrowed to constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy. Which laboratory finding would favor constrictive pericarditis?
opts: A very high natriuretic peptide leans toward restrictive cardiomyopathy or heart failure; constriction runs comparatively lower.
Sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are often elevated in constriction, so a normal value does not favor it.
Blood cultures point to infection such as endocarditis and do not separate constriction from restrictive disease.
Correct. No B-type natriuretic peptide threshold confirms or excludes constriction, but the level is likely lower in constrictive pericarditis than in restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 33-year-old man with typical acute pericarditis after a viral illness has a troponin that is above the reference range. Coronary angiography shows normal arteries. Which process does the troponin elevation most likely reflect?
opts: There is no reason to dismiss the value; in pericarditis an elevated troponin is read as myocardial involvement.
Correct. Troponin may be elevated if the myocardium is also affected, myopericarditis (perimyocarditis); an elevated troponin is also a feature that favors hospitalization.
His coronary arteries are normal, so troponin here reflects inflammation reaching the myocardium, not an occlusion.
ruled out by a stated finding
Constriction is a late, fibrotic process recognized by Kussmaul sign and imaging, not by troponin, which signals myocardial involvement.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 32-year-old man has typical acute viral pericarditis with stable vital signs and no high-risk features. A transthoracic echocardiogram is ordered. Which result is most expected?
opts: A normal study or only a small effusion
Correct. The echocardiogram is often normal in acute pericarditis unless there is an associated effusion, and the chest radiograph is typically normal; the diagnosis is primarily clinical.
Right ventricular diastolic collapse indicates tamponade, which this stable patient does not have.
A thick pericardium with septal bounce
Septal bounce with pericardial thickening suggests constrictive pericarditis, a late complication, not acute disease.
Apical ballooning with a normal base
Apical ballooning is stress cardiomyopathy. Acute pericarditis usually has a normal echocardiogram.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 59-year-old woman develops fever and positional chest pain with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) 2 weeks after a myocardial infarction treated with a coronary stent. Echocardiography shows a small effusion and her vital signs are stable. Which anti-inflammatory regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Pericarditis after a myocardial infarction (Dressler syndrome) is treated with aspirin as the anti-inflammatory plus colchicine; the other nonsteroidal drugs and glucocorticoids are avoided after infarction.
Indomethacin is a non-aspirin anti-inflammatory avoided in the peri-infarction setting. Aspirin plus colchicine is the regimen used for Dressler syndrome.
ruled out by a stated finding
Glucocorticoids are avoided in peri-infarction pericarditis and are second line elsewhere. Aspirin plus colchicine is preferred.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ibuprofen is first line for idiopathic or viral pericarditis but is avoided in post-infarction pericarditis, where aspirin is used instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 50-year-old man with acute pericarditis says the pain keeps him awake because it is worse when he lies down. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Sleep prone to splint the chest
Prone sleeping is not recommended. Elevating the head of the bed eases positional pericardial pain.
Take an extra dose at bedtime
Extra bedtime medication does not address positional pain; elevating the head of the bed eases it.
Keep the head of the bed elevated
Correct. Pericardial pain is worse supine and better leaning forward, so keeping the head of the bed elevated is advised, along with completing the full treatment course.
Sleep flat to rest the heart
Lying flat is exactly what worsens his pain. The head of the bed should be raised.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 71-year-old man with a new inferior myocardial infarction involving the right ventricle is hypotensive with distended jugular veins and clear lungs. Tamponade is considered. Why must his infarction stay on the differential?
opts: An infarction does not exclude tamponade; free-wall rupture after infarction can even cause it. It must be weighed as a mimic.
Infarction mimics acute tamponade; constriction, heart failure and cirrhosis mimic the subacute form.
Infarction is not the commonest cause of tamponade; it belongs here as a mimic and an occasional cause through rupture.
Correct. The differential of acute tamponade includes myocardial infarction (especially with right ventricular involvement), aortic dissection and massive pulmonary embolism, which can all mimic it.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has 2 days of worsening dyspnea and chest discomfort. Blood pressure is 84/56, heart rate 122, jugular veins are distended, and heart sounds are muffled. Her systolic pressure falls by 18 mmHg on inspiration (pulsus paradoxus, a systolic fall of more than 10 mmHg). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Hypotension, distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds (the Beck triad) with pulsus paradoxus and tachycardia in a patient with malignancy are cardiac tamponade, pericardial fluid under pressure compressing the heart.
Constriction develops over months with edema, ascites and the Kussmaul sign; it does not cause this acute hypotension with muffled sounds.
Acute pericarditis causes sharp positional pain and a rub; on its own it does not cause hypotension, jugular distension and pulsus paradoxus.
Tension pneumothorax gives absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation; muffled heart sounds with pulsus paradoxus point to tamponade.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 44-year-old man began having pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) pericardial pain 8 weeks ago. Despite treatment the symptoms have never fully gone away, with no symptom-free interval. Which term best describes his course?
opts: Chronic pericarditis requires symptoms for more than 3 months. At 8 weeks without remission the course is incessant.
ruled out by a stated finding
Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is persistent constriction after an effusion is drained, a structural diagnosis, not a time label.
Correct. Symptoms persisting beyond 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission define incessant pericarditis; past 3 months the label becomes chronic.
Recurrence needs a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before symptoms return; he has had no such interval.
ruled out by a stated finding

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 58-year-old man received chest radiation for lymphoma 20 years ago. He has 8 months of exertional dyspnea, fatigue, leg edema and ascites. His jugular venous pressure is elevated and shows the Kussmaul sign (it rises on inspiration instead of falling), and a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound, slightly earlier than a third heart sound) is heard. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute pericarditis presents with sharp pleuritic, positional pain and a friction rub, not months of edema, ascites and a Kussmaul sign.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes outflow obstruction and a systolic murmur, not a knock with a Kussmaul sign and ascites.
Endocarditis presents with fever, a new murmur and embolic signs, not the fluid overload and Kussmaul sign of constriction.

Correct. Fluid overload with low output, an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock after prior radiation are the picture of constrictive pericarditis, scarring that limits filling.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 59-year-old man with a large pericardial effusion is hypotensive and tachycardic. His electrocardiogram shows small QRS complexes with low voltage (small amplitude complexes) whose height alternates from beat to beat. Which electrocardiogram finding is this?
opts: Heart block drops ventricular beats after P waves; it does not make the QRS height alternate beat to beat.
PR depression with ST elevation is acute pericarditis; alternating QRS height is electrical alternans.
Correct. Electrical alternans, alternating QRS amplitude as the heart swings in the fluid, is fairly specific for tamponade and appears with low voltage and tachycardia.
Bigeminy is an ectopic beat after every normal beat, with a different QRS shape, not alternating height of identical complexes.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 48-year-old man becomes hypotensive and short of breath an hour after a catheter procedure perforates his heart. Echocardiogram shows only a small pericardial effusion, estimated at about 150 mL, with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Which best explains why so little fluid has compromised him?
opts: A pericardium that stretches over time lets a chronic effusion grow large without tamponade; here the fluid arrived fast into an unstretched sac, so under 200 mL was enough.
There is no need to assume a measurement error; small, rapid effusions can cause tamponade.
Calcification belongs to constriction. Here the problem is rapid fluid entry into a normal, unstretched sac.
Rapid filling of an unstretched sac
Correct. Acute effusions can produce tamponade with small amounts of fluid (under 200 mL) because the pericardium has no time to stretch, unlike chronic effusions that grow large over time.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 34-year-old man with acute pericarditis has taken ibuprofen and colchicine for 2 weeks. He has been symptom-free for 4 days, and his weekly C-reactive protein has just returned to normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Abrupt cessation risks recurrence. The anti-inflammatory is tapered, and colchicine continues for about 3 months.
He has responded fully; escalation is not needed. Tapering begins once he is symptom-free with a normal C-reactive protein.
Prednisone is second line for refractory disease or contraindications; he has responded and should taper.
Correct. With the C-reactive protein approach, tapering starts once the patient is symptom-free and the level has normalized; colchicine continues for about 3 months.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 41-year-old woman is being treated for acute pericarditis with an anti-inflammatory and colchicine. She asks whether she may take brisk walks while recovering. Which heart rate ceiling should guide her activity?
opts: A ceiling of 60 would demand bradycardia and is not the target. The limit is a maximal heart rate under 100.
Correct. During the restriction, strenuous activity is avoided and the maximal heart rate is kept under 100 beats per minute, for at least 1 month and until symptoms and C-reactive protein normalize.
One hundred fifty permits vigorous exercise, which the restriction forbids. The ceiling is under 100 beats per minute.
No limit if she feels well
Feeling well is not the guide; the heart rate stays under 100 until the inflammation and symptoms resolve.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 61-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease has a large pericardial effusion with stable blood pressure, and his blood urea nitrogen is 112 mg/dL. Which treatment addresses the cause?
opts: Antituberculous drugs treat tuberculous effusions; his kidney failure and very high urea point to a uremic effusion.
Steroids are the cause-directed therapy for autoimmune pericarditis, not uremic disease.
Pericardiectomy is for constriction and recurrent or loculated effusions, not first-line for uremic effusion.
Correct. Treating the underlying disorder is key; uremic pericarditis, associated with a blood urea nitrogen above 60 mg/dL, is treated with dialysis, and further management follows the cause.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 48-year-old woman is discharged on ibuprofen and colchicine for acute pericarditis. Which new symptom should prompt her to go straight to the emergency department rather than call for an appointment?
opts: Correct. Red-flag symptoms for tamponade or worsening disease, such as dyspnea, lightheadedness or falling exercise tolerance from low cardiac output, need emergency evaluation rather than a routine visit.
Mild fatigue in the late afternoon
Mild fatigue is common during recovery and is not a red flag. Lightheadedness with breathlessness suggests low cardiac output.
Pain that still eases on leaning forward
Persistent positional pain needs follow-up but is the expected pattern; hemodynamic symptoms are the emergency red flags.
Mild indigestion after doses of ibuprofen
Indigestion is a medication side effect to discuss and protect against; it is not a red flag for tamponade.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 60-year-old man with known malignant pericardial effusion has a blood pressure of 82/50, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus (an inspiratory systolic fall of 16 mmHg). Echocardiogram shows a large effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Which is the definitive treatment?
opts: Diuretics lower preload and can precipitate collapse in tamponade. Drainage is the definitive treatment.
Correct. Expedient pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade; it relieves the pressure and the fluid is sent for diagnostic studies.
Intravenous fluids raise preload and buy time, but they are temporizing; the fluid under pressure must be drained.
Anti-inflammatory therapy treats pericarditis but cannot relieve fluid under pressure in a hypotensive patient.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 69-year-old man has long-standing constrictive pericarditis with marked edema and ascites despite diuretics. A computed tomography scan shows a thick, heavily calcified pericardium. Which treatment offers definitive relief?
opts: Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is often a surgical disease; pericardiectomy, removal of part or most of the pericardium, is the definitive treatment and gives a 5-year survival near 80%.
Pericardiocentesis drains fluid and is the definitive treatment for tamponade. A thick, calcified pericardium must be removed surgically.
Anti-inflammatory therapy suits early, stable constriction; established calcified disease needs pericardiectomy.
The myocardium is not the problem in constriction. Removing the scarred pericardium is the definitive treatment.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for pericardial disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 9. adult 10. elderly
set1.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic kidney disease, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. His family asks what to expect. Which statement about his long-term outlook is most accurate?
opts: Age does not influence the outcome of surgery
Older adults carry higher morbidity and mortality with surgery, and older age itself predicts a poorer outcome.
His prognosis is as good as a young patient's
His age and comorbidities make the outlook worse than a younger, healthier patient's.
Survival without treatment is usually normal
Without treatment, survival in constrictive pericarditis is low, not normal; surgery improves it.
His age and comorbidities predict a worse outcome
Correct. Older age, worse functional class and comorbidities such as renal dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension and hyponatremia are independent predictors of poor long-term outcome in constriction.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 56-year-old woman has fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin and a heart rate of 54. Echocardiogram shows a large pericardial effusion without chamber collapse. Which test best addresses the cause her features suggest?
opts: Tuberculosis is a cause where it is prevalent, but her features point to myxedema. Thyroid tests fit.
Cultures look for bacterial infection. Her picture suggests hypothyroidism, tested with thyroid function tests.
Correct. Hypothyroidism (myxedema) is a metabolic cause of pericardial effusion, and thyroid function tests are part of the effusion workup; her symptoms point straight at it.
An antinuclear antibody screens for lupus; her cold intolerance, weight gain and bradycardia point to hypothyroidism.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 54-year-old man has a moderate-to-large pericardial effusion on echocardiogram with no hemodynamic compromise. Viral, uremic, thyroid and rheumatologic workups are unrevealing. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Pericardiectomy or a window is for recurrent or loculated effusions. First the cause should be found by sampling the fluid.

Correct. Diagnostic pericardiocentesis is considered for a moderate-to-large effusion of unknown etiology, as well as during therapeutic drainage for tamponade and with suspected neoplastic, purulent or tuberculous disease.
An unexplained moderate-to-large effusion needs a diagnosis; the fluid should be sampled rather than ignored.
Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for recurrent inflammatory pericarditis, not an undiagnosed effusion.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 38-year-old woman has her second recurrence of idiopathic pericarditis despite colchicine. Her temperature is 38.4 degrees Celsius, C-reactive protein is 45 mg/L, and cardiac magnetic resonance shows pericardial edema with late gadolinium enhancement. Which therapy is now preferred over corticosteroids?
opts: Azathioprine is a later-line immunosuppressant and not the preferred agent; anti-interleukin-1 therapy targets this inflammatory phenotype.
Surgery is considered for frequent, highly symptomatic recurrences or constriction, but a targeted anti-interleukin-1 trial comes before committing to it.

Correct. With an inflammatory phenotype (C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L, fever, imaging inflammation) and colchicine-resistant recurrence, an anti-interleukin-1 agent such as anakinra or rilonacept is preferred over corticosteroids.
Intravenous immunoglobulin is a later-line option on the older treatment table. For colchicine-resistant recurrence with an inflammatory phenotype, anti-interleukin-1 therapy is preferred.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 35-year-old woman has 3 days of sharp substernal chest pain that improves when she sits forward. Her vital signs are normal, and no rub is heard on careful auscultation. Which additional finding would complete the clinical diagnosis of acute pericarditis?
opts: Correct. The diagnosis needs two of four criteria: sharp substernal chest pain, a friction rub, suggestive electrocardiogram changes (widespread ST elevation) and a new or worsening effusion. Her pain plus the electrocardiogram would make two.
A troponin above the reference range
Troponin is not a diagnostic criterion; an elevated value would suggest myocardial involvement (myopericarditis) and higher risk.
The natriuretic peptide belongs to the constriction workup and is not a pericarditis criterion. Widespread ST elevation would complete the diagnosis.
Calcification points to long-standing constriction, not acute pericarditis, and is not one of the four criteria.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 58-year-old man with suspected tamponade has distended jugular veins and a blood pressure of 88/60. He has leg edema, and drainage is being arranged. Which drug class should be avoided?
opts: Local anesthesia is used for the pericardiocentesis itself and is not a concern here.
Antibiotics are not indicated for every tamponade, but they are not the harmful class here; diuretics are.
Correct. Fluid resuscitation is given in tamponade to increase preload and prevent right ventricular collapse, so diuretics, which reduce preload, should be avoided before drainage.
Intravenous fluids are the temporizing support in tamponade, raising preload until pericardiocentesis; they are not avoided.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 59-year-old man with a large pericardial effusion from metastatic cancer reports a hoarse voice, hiccups and difficulty swallowing. Which mechanism explains his hoarseness?
opts: Vena cava obstruction swells the face and arms; hoarseness comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Correct. Large effusions can cause dysphagia, nausea, hiccups, cough and hoarseness, the hoarseness from impingement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Direct invasion of the vocal cords
The effusion does not invade the larynx. It compresses the recurrent laryngeal nerve on its course through the chest.
The hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue and is far from the pericardium. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is impinged.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 45-year-old woman developed early signs of constriction 6 weeks after an episode of acute pericarditis. She is hemodynamically stable, and cardiac magnetic resonance shows pericardial edema with late gadolinium enhancement. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade from fluid under pressure. Early inflammatory constriction is treated medically first.
Untreated constriction carries low survival. A medical trial is appropriate for early, stable disease.

Correct. Early, hemodynamically stable constriction may get a trial of the acute pericarditis medicines for longer (2 to 3 months) with diuretics; edema or late enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance suggests reversible inflammation.
Committing to surgery is premature when imaging shows inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction in a stable patient.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: A 29-year-old woman has acute pericarditis with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound) and widespread ST elevation. Her clinician wants laboratory values that confirm inflammation and can guide the length of therapy. Which pair of tests is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. The initial workup includes complete blood count, troponins, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein; the C-reactive protein is checked at presentation and weekly to guide tapering.
D-dimer is not part of this workup and the natriuretic peptide is used in constriction. Inflammation is measured with sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.
Pancreatic and liver enzymes do not gauge pericardial inflammation. Sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein do.
Cultures are for suspected bacterial disease. Routine monitoring uses sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with ovarian cancer has had three drainages for a recurrent pericardial effusion, and the latest echocardiogram shows a loculated collection behind the heart. Which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Diuretics do not drain a malignant loculated effusion. A pericardial window does.
Correct. A pericardiectomy or pericardial window is performed for recurrent effusions and for loculated effusions, especially posterior ones that cannot be approached percutaneously.
A posterior loculated collection cannot be reached percutaneously, and repeat taps fail with recurrence; a window is needed.
Thoracentesis drains the pleural space, not the pericardium. A pericardial window is the procedure.

set1.q: A 60-year-old woman with confirmed constrictive pericarditis has failed a 3-month trial of anti-inflammatories and diuretics and remains fluid overloaded. Which service performs the definitive procedure she needs?
opts: Nephrology helps with uremic pericardial disease, not with removing a constrictive pericardium.
Correct. Constriction refractory to medical therapy needs pericardiectomy, an operation performed by cardiothoracic surgery working with cardiology.
Radiology may drain some collections, but removing the pericardium is cardiothoracic surgery.
Her ascites mimics cirrhosis, but the cause is cardiac; pericardiectomy is cardiothoracic surgery.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman is diagnosed with constrictive pericarditis. She had mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 25 years ago and is otherwise well. Which feature of her history most worsens her long-term prognosis?
opts: Correct. Etiology is an important determinant of survival in constrictive pericarditis, and prior ionizing radiation is associated with the worst survival rates.
Sex is not named as a determinant of survival. Prior ionizing radiation carries the worst prognosis.
Comorbidities worsen the outlook, so their absence helps. Her prior radiation is what worsens it.
The lymphoma itself is cured; it is the radiation used to treat it that predicts the worst survival.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer has a symptomatic malignant pericardial effusion that has already reaccumulated once after drainage. Which consult is recommended to improve her outcomes and quality of life?
opts: Endocrinology addresses thyroid causes such as myxedema. Palliative care is recommended here.

Correct. Symptomatic malignant pericardial effusion carries a limited life expectancy (median 2 to 4 months) and often recurs; a palliative care consult is recommended to improve outcomes and quality of life.
Physical therapy may help mobility, but the recommended consult for a symptomatic malignant effusion is palliative care.
Rheumatology helps autoimmune effusions. A malignant effusion calls for palliative care.

set2.q: A 31-year-old man was treated for acute pericarditis 3 months ago and has been symptom-free for 6 weeks. His sharp, positional chest pain has now returned with a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). C-reactive protein is mildly raised. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Anti-interleukin-1 therapy is for colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent recurrence with a strong inflammatory phenotype, not a first recurrence.
Ibuprofen with colchicine for 6 months or more

Correct. This is a first recurrence, symptoms returning after a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer, treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine for 6 months or more.
Ibuprofen with colchicine, stopped at 2 weeks
Two weeks of colchicine is far too short after a recurrence; the course is 6 months or more.
Prednisone alone is not the recurrence regimen; when used it is given with colchicine. Anti-inflammatory plus colchicine for 6 months or more comes first.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 52-year-old man has had 10 days of gradually worsening pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain without a clear onset. His temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius (101.7 degrees Fahrenheit), and the echocardiogram shows a moderate pericardial effusion without collapse of any chamber. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassurance and repeat echo in 3 months
Waiting months with fever and a moderate effusion is unsafe; these high-risk features call for admission and evaluation now.
Pericardiectomy is for recurrent or loculated effusions and constriction, not a first presentation. He needs admission and workup.
Correct. Fever above 38 degrees Celsius, a subacute course over days to weeks and a moderate to large effusion are all high-risk features that favor hospitalization and further evaluation.
Outpatient therapy suits low-risk disease. His fever, subacute course and moderate effusion are high-risk features that favor admission.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 76-year-old woman has needed prednisone for several months for pericarditis that did not respond to first-line therapy. Which complication of her treatment should be specifically anticipated?
opts: Corticosteroids tend to raise blood glucose rather than lower it. Osteoporosis is the specific concern in older adults.
Bradycardia is not a corticosteroid effect named here. Osteoporosis is the anticipated complication.
Hearing loss is not a recognized steroid concern in this setting; osteoporosis is.
Correct. Corticosteroids increase the risk of osteoporosis, a particular concern in older adults on prolonged courses, so bone health must be addressed.

set2.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with acute idiopathic pericarditis after a viral illness. He is afebrile, his troponin is normal, the echocardiogram shows no effusion, and he has no contraindication to any medication. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as ibuprofen plus colchicine is the initial recommended therapy for most acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis, with gastrointestinal protection.
Prednisone is second line, for refractory cases or patients who cannot take nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; he has no such contraindication.
Anakinra is reserved for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease with an inflammatory phenotype, not a first uncomplicated episode.
Antibiotics have no role in idiopathic or viral pericarditis; they are for bacterial infection. An anti-inflammatory plus colchicine is first line.

set2.q: A 27-year-old woman recovering well from her first episode of acute viral pericarditis asks how likely it is to come back. Which estimate is most accurate?
opts: Recurrence is much more common than 1%; about 15 to 30% of patients have another episode.
Correct. Recurrent pericarditis affects about 15 to 30% of patients after acute pericarditis, which is why completing the full course and recognizing symptoms early matter.
Sixty percent overstates the risk. About 15 to 30% of patients have a recurrence.
Recurrence is common but far from universal: it follows about 15 to 30% of acute episodes, so most patients never have a second episode.

set2.q: A 27-year-old woman has a new moderate pericardial effusion with joint aches and fatigue. She has not traveled and has no recent viral illness. Which test is most reasonable to add to her workup?
opts: Correct. The effusion workup includes blood counts, chemistry, thyroid-stimulating hormone and troponins, and possibly an antinuclear antibody, for example in a young woman with an effusion, to look for lupus.
Blood cultures look for a bacterial infection, which nothing in her story suggests. Joint aches and fatigue in a young woman point to lupus, so an antinuclear antibody is added.
Lipase looks for pancreatitis and has no role in an effusion workup. An antinuclear antibody does.
A1c measures diabetes control and does not explain an effusion. An antinuclear antibody screens for lupus.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man is discharged after a large viral pericardial effusion was found without tamponade. He asks how the effusion will be monitored. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. All large pericardial effusions should be followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms, with close clinical follow-up by the specialty matching the cause.
An electrocardiogram cannot measure fluid. Serial transthoracic echocardiograms follow a large effusion.
Radiographs show only gross enlargement. Serial echocardiograms are the follow-up for large effusions.
Large effusions can reaccumulate; serial echocardiograms are recommended even when symptoms settle.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman had a large effusion drained for tamponade. Afterward her jugular venous pressure remains elevated and shows the Kussmaul sign (a rise on inspiration), and she remains fluid overloaded. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Effusive-constrictive pericarditis is underlying constriction with a coexisting effusion, usually with tamponade, in which constriction persists after the effusion is drained.
Recurrence is a return of pericarditis symptoms after a symptom-free gap of 4 to 6 weeks, not persistent constriction right after drainage.
A simple effusion resolves once drained; persistent constrictive physiology afterward is effusive-constrictive disease.
ruled out by a stated finding
Restrictive cardiomyopathy can mimic constriction, but constriction that persists right after a tamponading effusion is drained defines effusive-constrictive pericarditis.

set2.q: A 40-year-old woman with right lower lobe pneumonia has sharp chest pain. A rubbing sound is heard over the lower chest that is present only while she breathes in and vanishes when she holds her breath. Which is the most likely source of the sound?
opts: A pericardial rub continues, and gets louder, when the breath is held, because only the heart is moving. This sound stopped with breath-holding.
ruled out by a stated finding
Valve murmurs do not disappear with breath-holding and are not rubs. This is a pleural rub.
Chest wall pain is reproducible on palpation and makes no rubbing sound. A rub that stops with breath-holding is pleural.
Correct. A pleural rub is tied to respiration, heard in the inspiratory phase, and disappears with breath-holding; a pericardial rub persists, and even intensifies, while the breath is held.

set2.q: A 35-year-old man who recently moved from a region where tuberculosis is common has effusive pericarditis. Pericardial fluid is positive on acid-fast stain. Which treatment may significantly reduce his progression to constriction?
opts: Correct. If tuberculosis is the underlying etiology, treatment of the tuberculosis may significantly reduce progression to constrictive pericarditis.
Pericardiectomy treats established constriction; treating the tuberculosis is what reduces progression to it.
Diuretics relieve fluid overload but leave the infection untreated. Antituberculous therapy reduces progression.
Aspirin treats inflammation, not the mycobacterial infection driving the scarring. Antituberculous therapy does.

set2.q: A 67-year-old former smoker with weight loss has a large pericardial effusion. Lung cancer is suspected, and pericardiocentesis is performed. Which study of the pericardial fluid best addresses this suspicion?
opts: Gram stain looks for bacteria in purulent pericarditis, not for cancer cells. Cytology does.
Fungal culture detects fungal infection, not malignancy. Cytology addresses suspected lung cancer.
Cell count and differential are rarely helpful in establishing the diagnosis. Cytology looks for malignant cells.
Correct. Pericardial fluid is sent for cell count, Gram stain, cultures, acid-fast studies and cytology, and cytology is the study that identifies malignant cells.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with advanced constrictive pericarditis and moderate biatrial enlargement reports new palpitations. His pulse is irregularly irregular. Which rhythm is he most prone to?
opts: Complete heart block is slow and regular, not irregularly irregular, and is not the rhythm linked to constriction.
ruled out by a stated finding
Ventricular tachycardia is regular and wide; atrial fibrillation is the common rhythm of advanced constriction.

Correct. Atrial fibrillation is common in advanced constrictive pericarditis, encouraged by biatrial enlargement; nonspecific ST and T-wave changes, tachycardia and low voltage are the other findings.
Flutter is usually regular. An irregularly irregular pulse in advanced constriction is atrial fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman with tamponade from a newly found effusion and no known cancer is being evaluated. Which consideration about the cause is most important at her age?
opts: Dressler syndrome follows myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery, which she has not had.
Her age makes the cause irrelevant
The cause drives long-term prognosis and management; at her age malignancy deserves particular attention.
Correct. Older adults with an effusion or tamponade warrant a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, while younger patients are more often idiopathic or viral.
Coxsackievirus is a classic viral cause, usually after a viral illness. At her age, with tamponade and no known cause, malignancy should be suspected more strongly.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 44-year-old man had a tuberculous pericardial effusion drained in the hospital and is starting antituberculous therapy. Which specialty should be part of his close follow-up?
opts: Correct. Close clinical follow-up is tailored to the underlying etiology: cardiology, infectious disease, nephrology, oncology or rheumatology; a tuberculous effusion calls for infectious disease.
Nephrology follows a uremic effusion in kidney failure. A tuberculous effusion on antituberculous therapy is followed closely with infectious disease.
Rheumatology follows an autoimmune effusion such as lupus. His tuberculous effusion is followed by infectious disease, which guides antituberculous therapy.
Medical oncology follows a malignant effusion. A tuberculous effusion on antituberculous therapy is followed closely with infectious disease.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 58-year-old man with acute pericarditis is starting ibuprofen and colchicine. He has a history of dyspepsia. Which addition to his regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Anticoagulation is not part of pericarditis therapy, and patients already on anticoagulants are a higher-risk group.
Antibiotics have no role in idiopathic or viral pericarditis. Gastrointestinal protection is the needed addition.
Diuretics treat fluid overload in constrictive disease, not acute pericarditis. He needs gastrointestinal protection.
Correct. Gastrointestinal protection is provided with anti-inflammatory therapy, for example a proton pump inhibitor, because these drugs reduce the stomach's protective prostaglandins.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 26-year-old marathon runner is diagnosed with acute viral pericarditis and starts ibuprofen and colchicine. He asks when he can return to training. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Run on alternate days during treatment
Even alternate-day running exceeds the restriction, which keeps the heart rate under 100 until the inflammation settles.
Avoid exercise for the rest of his life
Lifelong restriction is not advised; he avoids strenuous activity for at least 1 month and until biomarkers normalize.
Avoid strenuous activity for at least 1 month
Correct. Strenuous activity should be avoided until symptoms resolve and biomarkers such as C-reactive protein normalize, at least 1 month after diagnosis, keeping the maximal heart rate under 100.
Resume running once the chest pain stops
Pain resolution alone is not enough; restriction lasts at least 1 month and until C-reactive protein normalizes.

set2.q: A 36-year-old woman has had three episodes of pericarditis in 18 months, each treated in primary care with an anti-inflammatory and colchicine. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Surgery is not the first referral for recurrence; cardiology assesses it and decides whether advanced therapy or surgery is needed.
Correct. Referral to cardiology is advised for recurrences (recurrent pericarditis), for no response to conservative management and for the development of constrictive pericarditis.
Infectious disease input is for proven or suspected infection such as tuberculosis or purulent disease; recurrence itself is a cardiology referral.
Gastroenterology may help with anti-inflammatory side effects, but recurrent pericarditis is referred to cardiology.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 57-year-old man with constrictive pericarditis is scheduled for pericardiectomy next week. He takes a loop diuretic for leg edema. How should the diuretic be handled before surgery?
opts: Adding diuretics intensifies volume depletion before surgery. Diuretics should be used sparingly.
Correct. If surgery is planned, diuretics should be used sparingly in the preoperative period, even though they relieve the fluid overload of constriction.
Aggressive diuresis before pericardiectomy is advised against; diuretics are used sparingly preoperatively.
No route change is recommended; the guidance for the preoperative period is to use diuretics sparingly.

set2.q: A 61-year-old woman with recurrent pericarditis over several years now has leg edema, ascites and an elevated jugular venous pressure. Constrictive pericarditis is suspected. Which echocardiogram finding would best support it?
opts: Right ventricular diastolic collapse is the echocardiographic sign of tamponade, from fluid under pressure, not constriction.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Constriction shows a septal bounce and a thick pericardium.
A dilated, poorly contracting ventricle is dilated cardiomyopathy; constriction keeps systolic function and restricts filling.
Septal bounce toward the left ventricle

Correct. Echocardiographic features of constriction are increased pericardial thickness, abnormal septal motion or bounce toward the left ventricle, pronounced respiratory variation in ventricular filling and moderate biatrial enlargement.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 66-year-old man is readmitted 3 weeks after coronary artery bypass surgery with fever, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain eased by sitting forward, and a friction rub (a scratchy, squeaking sound). His sternal wound looks clean. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Pericarditis weeks after myocardial infarction or post-cardiotomy (cardiac surgery) is Dressler syndrome, an inflammatory reaction to the injured tissue; aspirin plus colchicine treats it.
His wound looks clean, and a wound infection does not produce a friction rub with positional pericardial pain.
ruled out by a stated finding
Graft occlusion causes ischemic pressure pain and regional changes, not positional pain with a rub.
Constriction is a later scarring process presenting with fluid overload and low output, not acute pleuritic pain with fever and a rub.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman is hypotensive with distended neck veins and a large effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse. After pericardiocentesis removes 600 mL, her blood pressure rises from 80/50 to 118/74 and her dyspnea resolves. What does this response establish?
opts: Persistent constriction after drainage would suggest effusive-constrictive pericarditis; her full recovery fits tamponade.
It shows the echo was misread
Her response confirms what the bedside picture and echo suggested, tamponade, rather than discrediting the echo.
Correct. Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis; echocardiography identifies the effusion and its significance, but the diagnosis is confirmed only by the hemodynamic and clinical response to drainage.
It rules out a malignant cause
Improvement after drainage says nothing about the cause; the fluid must still be sent for cytology and other studies.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 40-year-old woman has taken ibuprofen and colchicine for 8 days for presumed viral pericarditis. She still has a temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius and pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) pain, and a new pericardial effusion has appeared on echocardiogram. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Stop colchicine and add a diuretic
Diuretics treat fluid overload in constriction, and stopping colchicine removes useful therapy. She needs evaluation for another cause.
Start anakinra as a first step
Anakinra is for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease with an inflammatory phenotype; first she needs a search for a specific cause.
Admit and look for another cause

Correct. Persistent fever and pain with a new effusion define treatment failure, and failure to respond within 1 week suggests a cause other than idiopathic or viral; no improvement after 7 days favors hospitalization.
Continue the same drugs for a month
Continuing unchanged ignores treatment failure. No response by 1 week calls for admission and a search for a specific cause.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 55-year-old man has fatigue, exertional dyspnea, an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign (a rise on inspiration), ascites and minimal ankle edema. His liver enzymes are mildly raised. Which condition is the key noncardiac mimic to consider?
opts: Hyperthyroidism is not a mimic of constriction; hypothyroidism appears instead as a cause of effusion.

Correct. Cirrhosis is in the differential of constrictive pericarditis because both cause ascites and fluid overload; an elevated jugular venous pressure with the Kussmaul sign points back to the heart.
Asthma causes wheeze and dyspnea, not ascites with a raised jugular venous pressure.
Pneumonia is a differential of acute pericarditis chest pain, not the fluid-overloaded picture of constriction.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: A 64-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, pleuritic (worse with a deep breath) chest pain eased by sitting forward, and a friction rub (a scratchy, three-part rubbing sound) at the left sternal border. Which drug should be avoided in treating his pericarditis?
opts: Aspirin is exactly the anti-inflammatory used for post-infarction pericarditis, continued from his infarction care, with colchicine added.
Colchicine is added to aspirin for post-infarction pericarditis; it is part of the treatment, not a drug to avoid.
A proton pump inhibitor such as pantoprazole gives the gastrointestinal protection that anti-inflammatory therapy calls for; it is not avoided.

Correct. This is post-infarction (Dressler) pericarditis, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen are not given after a myocardial infarction; glucocorticoids are also avoided. Aspirin plus colchicine is used.

set2.q: A 39-year-old man who grew up in a country where tuberculosis is common has fever, night sweats and a moderate pericardial effusion. Fluid is obtained by pericardiocentesis. Which fluid studies best address the suspected cause?
opts: Routine stains and cultures miss mycobacteria; an acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture are needed.
Antinuclear antibody is a blood test for lupus. Tuberculosis is sought with acid-fast studies.
Correct. Pericardial fluid is sent for an acid-fast bacilli stain and mycobacterial culture to identify tuberculosis, alongside cell count, Gram stain, cultures and cytology.
Cytology looks for cancer. Suspected tuberculosis needs an acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture.

set2.q: An 81-year-old man with 3 months of weight loss presents with dyspnea and a large pericardial effusion. He has had no recent viral illness, chest surgery or radiation. Which etiology should be most strongly suspected?
opts: Dressler syndrome follows myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery, which he has not had.
ruled out by a stated finding
Rheumatic pancarditis follows streptococcal infection in younger patients and is not the concern here; malignancy is.
Correct. In older adults there is a higher index of suspicion for malignancy, especially with an effusion or tamponade, and his weight loss without a viral prodrome reinforces it.
Coxsackievirus is a classic cause of viral pericarditis and would usually follow a viral illness, which he has not had. Malignancy fits this older man.

set2.q: A 62-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 2 years ago has 3 weeks of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. Her blood pressure is 128/80 without hypotension. The chest radiograph shows an enlarged, water-bottle (globular) cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Which test is required to confirm a pericardial effusion?
opts: A radiograph suggested the effusion with a globular silhouette but cannot confirm it. Echocardiography is required.
Low voltage may hint at fluid, but the electrocardiogram cannot confirm an effusion. Echocardiography can.
Angiography images the coronary arteries, not the pericardial space. Echocardiography confirms an effusion.
Correct. Clinical evaluation, electrocardiogram and chest radiograph may suggest a pericardial effusion, but an echocardiogram is required to confirm it and to assess its hemodynamic significance.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with renal failure has a large pericardial effusion and borderline blood pressure. His chest radiograph shows a markedly enlarged, water-bottle (globular) cardiac silhouette. What do his lung fields most likely show?
opts: Consolidation indicates pneumonia; the effusion picture is a globular heart with clear lungs.
Correct. A large effusion gives cardiomegaly with a globular, water-bottle silhouette, and the lung fields may be clear, unlike the congestion of heart failure.
Bat-wing edema reflects left heart failure; an effusion classically enlarges the silhouette with clear lungs.
Hilar adenopathy suggests sarcoidosis or lymphoma and is not the radiograph of a large effusion.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man comes to a primary care office with dyspnea, lightheadedness, distended neck veins and a blood pressure of 86/58. He was diagnosed with a pericardial effusion last month. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A delayed referral is unsafe; signs of tamponade mean immediate transfer to the emergency department.
Send him to the emergency department
Correct. Evidence suggesting cardiac tamponade is a high-risk feature that requires hospitalization, and tamponade is an emergency, so he goes to the emergency department now.
An outpatient study delays care for possible tamponade, which is an emergency needing hospital evaluation now.
Anti-inflammatory therapy cannot relieve tamponade; he needs emergency evaluation and likely pericardiocentesis.
